Ross C.lab_name: Ross Lab, Southwest National Primate Research Center, Texas Biomedical Research Institute (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ross C.role: Primate biologist at Texas Biomedical Research Institute who uses the common marmoset to test whether drugs such as rapamycin can protect health during aging
Ross C.sub: Professor and Principal Investigator, Texas Biomedical Research Institute · Associate Director for Research, Southwest National Primate Research Center · earlier at the Barshop Institute, UT Health San Antonio, and Texas A&M University San Antonio (PubMed affiliation 2014–2016) · postdoc in the Biology of Aging, UT Health San Antonio · PhD in Biological Sciences, University of Nebraska-Lincoln (2005)
story: Rapamycin extends life in mice, but no one knows yet whether it does the same in primates. The common marmoset, a small South American monkey that lives about 10 to 15 years, is a practical test case. Corinna Ross was first author of the 2015 Atlas study (ROS2015) on long-term oral rapamycin in marmosets. Body weight, daily activity, blood fats and glucose handling barely changed, so the metabolic side effects that worry people about the drug were small in these animals. In the liver, one enzyme that makes glucose (G6Pase) became less active.

Ross is also a co-author of the 2014 study that first worked out how to dose rapamycin in marmosets (TAR2014) and of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016). These three papers belong to a longer San Antonio project that set up the marmoset as a model for testing anti-aging drugs.

Ross studied biology at Cornell University and the University of Nebraska Omaha, earned a PhD in biological sciences at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln in 2005, and trained as a postdoctoral Biology of Aging fellow at UT Health San Antonio. At the time of these studies PubMed lists Ross at the Barshop Institute and at Texas A&M University San Antonio. Ross now runs a laboratory as Professor at Texas Biomedical Research Institute and is Associate Director for Research at the Southwest National Primate Research Center, still using marmosets to study interventions for healthy aging.

highlights.ROS2015: First author: showed that long-term oral rapamycin had only minor metabolic effects in common marmosets.
highlights.TAR2014: Co-author: part of the team that first described rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author: contributed marmoset tissue work to the study of proteasome, chaperone and autophagy changes under rapamycin.

Ross C.note: Texas Biomed page uses she/her, but the text avoids pronouns. Full name with middle initial (Corinna N. Ross) from PubMed 2025.

Tardif S.lab_name: Southwest National Primate Research Center, Texas Biomedical Research Institute (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Tardif S.role: Primate biologist who spent more than 30 years developing the common marmoset as a research model, and who led the first studies of rapamycin dosing and safety in this small monkey
Tardif S.sub: Scientist and Associate Director of Primate Research, Texas Biomedical Research Institute · Associate Director of Research, Southwest National Primate Research Center · Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (PubMed affiliation 2014–2016)
story: Suzette Tardif was first author of the 2014 Atlas study (TAR2014) that first described how to give rapamycin to the common marmoset. The drug was put in a protective coating and fed by mouth at about 1 mg per kg each day. Blood levels were similar to those in mouse aging studies and within the range used in human medicine. In treated animals, the marker of mTORC1 activity, the growth-control complex, fell in blood cells, liver and fat. The monkeys showed no anemia, lung scarring or mouth ulcers, side effects known from patients on the drug.

Tardif was senior author of the 2015 follow-up (ROS2015), which found only minor metabolic effects of long-term treatment, and a co-author of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016). Together these papers made the marmoset a usable model for testing anti-aging drugs in a primate, though none of them measured lifespan.

Tardif's research covers metabolism, behaviour and reproduction in marmosets, and more recently their use as a model of obesity and aging. A 2025 study with Corinna Ross on predicting obesity and blood-sugar problems in adult marmosets lists Tardif at the Southwest National Primate Research Center of Texas Biomedical Research Institute, where Tardif has served as Associate Director of Research.

highlights.TAR2014: First author: first described oral rapamycin dosing, blood levels and mTORC1 inhibition in common marmosets.
highlights.ROS2015: Senior author: led the study showing only minor metabolic effects of long-term rapamycin in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author: provided the marmoset cohort for the study of proteasome and autophagy markers under rapamycin.

Tardif S.note: Current title taken from a Newswise expert profile (undated); 2025 PubMed affiliation confirms Texas Biomed/SNPRC. PhD details not found. Newswise uses 'she'; text avoids pronouns.

Nelson G.lab_name: Bioimaging Unit, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Nelson G.role: Microscopy specialist who manages Newcastle University's Bioimaging Unit and has worked for many years on the signalling networks that keep senescent cells in their arrested state
Nelson G.sub: Specialist Experimental Scientific Officer and manager, Bioimaging Unit, Newcastle University · postdoc with Thomas von Zglinicki, Newcastle University · postdocs at the University of Liverpool and AstraZeneca · BSc and PhD, University of Edinburgh
story: Senescent cells have stopped dividing for good but stay alive and active, and they build up in aging tissues. Glyn Nelson is a co-author of two Newcastle studies in this Atlas that look at how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, behaves in these cells. The 2017 paper (CAR2017), on which Nelson is second author, found that mTORC1 stays switched on in senescent human fibroblasts and no longer responds when nutrients or growth factors are taken away. The fault lies upstream of mTORC1, in how the cells sense amino acids and growth signals. The 2024 paper (KEL2024) found that the routine clearing of damaged mitochondria shuts down as cells become senescent or old. Both studies were done in cultured human cells.

Nelson studied at the University of Edinburgh for a BSc and a PhD, then worked as a postdoc at AstraZeneca and at the University of Liverpool, and later joined Thomas von Zglinicki's group at Newcastle, which studies cell senescence. That research thread, on the signalling networks that start and maintain senescence, continues alongside Nelson's imaging role.

Nelson now manages Newcastle University's Bioimaging Unit, which gives researchers across the university access to light microscopes, training and image analysis help. Nelson also develops standard quality-control methods for light microscopy with the international QUAREP-LiMi initiative.

highlights.CAR2017: Second author: contributed to the study showing that mTORC1 stays active in senescent human cells because nutrient and growth-factor sensing upstream of it is faulty.
highlights.KEL2024: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that basal mitophagy shuts down in senescent and aged human cells.

Nelson G.note: Previous profile used 'him'; pronoun removed because the staff page does not state it.

Kelly G.lab_name: Korolchuk Lab, Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Kelly G.role: Cell biologist from Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University who showed that the routine clearing of damaged mitochondria fails as human cells become senescent
Kelly G.sub: Biosciences Institute, Newcastle University (PubMed affiliation 2020–2024, Korolchuk lab, at the time of the study)
story: Mitochondria are the power stations of the cell, and damaged ones are removed by a process called mitophagy. George Kelly is first author of the 2024 Developmental Cell study in this Atlas (KEL2024). In healthy primary human cells, mitophagy ran at a steady high level, started by superoxide made in the mitochondria and carried out through the PINK1/Parkin pathway with p62 as the receptor that tags mitochondria for removal. This housekeeping shut down when cells became senescent, the non-dividing state that builds up with age, and in cells from older donors. Blocking mitophagy in young cells was enough to push them into senescence.

The study also matters for rapamycin. Turning mitophagy back on was needed for rapamycin and NAD precursors to hold back senescence, which suggests that part of rapamycin's effect on cell aging works through mitochondrial quality control. A small molecule that targets p62 could restore mitophagy and reverse aging features in the cells. All of this was shown in cultured human cells.

PubMed links Kelly to Viktor Korolchuk's group at Newcastle University from 2020, starting with a review on reactive oxygen species and autophagy in neurons. Kelly is also a co-author of a 2022 Developmental Cell paper from the same lab showing that autophagy keeps cells alive by maintaining NAD levels, of a 2022 eLife study on short senolytic treatments in irradiated mice, and of a 2023 Nature paper with Joao Passos on how stressed senescent cells release mitochondrial DNA. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.KEL2024: First author: showed that basal mitophagy shuts down in senescent and aged human cells and that its return is needed for rapamycin's anti-senescence effect.

Kelly G.note: No staff or thesis page found; position is the PubMed affiliation up to 2024.
